sourceSentences.text: “It’s the oldest rule in the book,” said the King.
“Then it ought to be Number One,” said Alice.
The King turned pale, and shut his note-book hastily.
“Consider your verdict,” he said to the jury, in a low trembling voice.
“There’s more evidence to come yet, please your Majesty,” said the White Rabbit, jumping up in a great hurry: “this paper has just been picked up.”
“What’s in it?” said the Queen.
“I haven’t opened it yet,” said the White Rabbit; “but it seems to be a letter, written by the prisoner to—to somebody.”
“It must have been that,” said the King, “unless it was written to nobody, which isn’t usual, you know.”
“Who is it directed to?” said one of the jurymen.
“It isn’t directed at all,” said the White Rabbit; “in fact, there’s nothing written on the outside.”
He unfolded the paper as he spoke, and added “It isn’t a letter, after all: it’s a set of verses.”
“Are they in the prisoner’s handwriting?” asked another of the jurymen.
“No, they’re not,” said the White Rabbit, “and that’s the queerest thing about it.”
(The jury all looked puzzled.)
“He must have imitated somebody else’s hand,” said the King.
(The jury all brightened up again.)
“Please your Majesty,” said the Knave, “I didn’t write it, and they ca’n’t prove I did: there’s no name signed at the end.”
“If you didn’t sign it,” said the King, “that only makes the matter worse.
You must have meant some mischief, or else you’d have signed your name like an honest man.”
There was a general clapping of hands at this: it was the first really clever thing the King had said that day.
“That proves his guilt, of course,” said the Queen: “so, off with—”
“It doesn’t prove anything of the sort!” said Alice.
“Why, you don’t even know what they’re about!”
“Read them,” said the King.
The White Rabbit put on his spectacles.
“Where shall I begin, please your Majesty?” he asked.
“Begin at the beginning,” the King said, very gravely, “and go on till you come to the end: then stop.”
There was dead silence in the court, whilst the White Rabbit read out these verses:—
“They told me you had been to her,
And mentioned me to him:
She gave me a good character,
But said I could not swim.
He sent them word I had not gone
(We know it to be true):
If she should push the matter on,
What would become of you?
I gave her one, they gave him two,
You gave us three or more;
They all returned from him to you,
Though they were mine before.
If I or she should chance to be
Involved in this affair,
He trusts to you to set them free,
Exactly as we were.
My notion was that you had been
(Before she had this fit)
An obstacle that came between
Him, and ourselves, and it.
Don’t let him know she liked them best,
For this must ever be
A secret, kept from all the rest,
Between yourself and me.”
“That’s the most important piece of evidence we’ve heard yet,” said the King, rubbing his hands; “so now let the jury—”

— Ничего подобного это не доказывает! — сказала Алиса.
— Да ведь вы даже не знаете, о чём они!
— Прочтите их, — сказал Король.
Белый Кролик надел очки.
— С чего мне начать, с позволения вашего величества? — спросил он.
«Начни с начала, — очень важно сказал Король, — и продолжай, пока не дойдёшь до конца: тогда остановись.»
В суде воцарилась мёртвая тишина, пока Белый Кролик читал следующие стихи: —
«Мне сказали: ты была у неё,
И обо мне ему говорила;
Она дала мне добрую характеристику,
Но сказала, что плавать я не умела.
Он передал им, что я не ходила
(Мы знаем: это правда):
А если она поведёт это дело дальше,
Что тогда будет с тобой?
Я дала ей одну, они дали ему две,
Ты дала нам три или больше;
Все они вернулись от него к тебе,
Хотя прежде были моими.
Если мне или ей случится быть
Замешанными в этом деле,
Он надеется, что ты их освободишь,
Совсем как были мы сами.
Я полагала, что ты была
(До того как у неё случился припадок)
Препятствием, вставшим между
Ним, нами и этим.
Не дай ему узнать, что они ей нравились больше всего,
Ибо это навеки должно остаться
Тайной, скрытой от всех прочих,
Между тобой и мной.»
